title: Low-key UK Budget kicks the can into 2027
gist: Oxford Economics sees the UK Budget as a low-key, market-calming package of temporary cost-of-living measures that defers real fiscal reform to 2027, with lower headroom judged acceptable. It plans to raise its 2027 growth forecast on AI-intensive sector strength, doubts planned tax rises will deliver the hoped-for deficit reduction, and leaves regional forecasts unchanged after thin devolution announcements.

themes.theme: Budget as a market-calming holding pattern

insights.claim: The UK Budget was a deliberately low-key event designed to keep gilt markets onside, deferring a comprehensive overhaul of fiscal policy to 2027; the near-term measures are temporary cost-of-living support.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Little fiscal-policy surprise risk now; the real repricing event for gilts and sterling is shifted to 2027.
insights.quote: The UK Budget presented recently was a low-key event aimed at keeping markets onside ahead of a more comprehensive overhaul of fiscal policy in 2027.

insights.claim: The temporary cost-of-living measures give only a small near-term growth boost, and Oxford Economics was already planning to raise its 2027 UK growth forecast because of sustained strength in AI-intensive sectors, so the upgrade is driven by AI rather than fiscal policy.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: UK growth upside is attributed to AI-linked sectors, not Budget stimulus, so it depends on AI sector momentum.
insights.quote: we’d already planned to raise our forecast for 2027 due to the recent sustained strength of AI-intensive sectors

insights.claim: Running with lower fiscal headroom is judged a sensible compromise because it is unclear whether high gilt yields will persist and fiscal policy is likely to be reshaped next year; Oxford expects markets to be comfortable with it.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Thin headroom is tolerable only while gilt yields stay contained; a persistent yield spike would make the choice look fragile.
insights.quote: The decision to run with lower headroom looks like a sensible compromise given the uncertainty over whether high gilt yields will persist

insights.claim: Oxford Economics has major doubts that the planned tax rises will deliver the scale of deficit reduction the government hopes for over the next few years, implying fiscal-consolidation shortfall risk beyond the Budget.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Risk of renewed fiscal gaps and gilt supply concerns, and pressure for further tax or spending action in 2027.
insights.quote: we still have major doubts that the planned tax rises will deliver the scale of deficit reduction that the government hopes

insights.claim: The devolution announcements are too thin on detail, leave challenges unaddressed and would take a long time to pay off, so Oxford Economics will not revise its UK regional forecasts.
insights.speaker: Duncan Campbell
insights.so_what: Devolution is not a near-term regional growth catalyst; do not price regional upside from the announcements.
insights.quote: the devolution announcements will not lead us to revising our regional forecasts
